title: Benchmark Report Core Messaging (Latency per $ / Production Economics)
author: Soojin Lee
content:
## Purpose
This page is the single source of truth for how Redwood Inference talks about the **Latency per Dollar (Latency/$)** benchmark report externally and in the field.

Use it to:
- Keep **Marketing, Sales, SE, CS, and Support** aligned on *what we say* and *what we do not say*.
- Explain “production economics” to both **engineers** and **procurement** without over-claiming.
- Select **headline stats** that are accurate, defensible, and consistent with the public report.

**If you need to deviate from this language (e.g., custom customer claim, naming a competitor, citing unpublished numbers), route through:** Jordan Blake + Markus Klein + Michael Grant.

---
## TL;DR (what we’re saying)
**Redwood Inference is positioning as the credible reference for production economics in LLM serving.**

We are publishing a benchmark report that:
- Measures **latency, throughput, cost, and Latency/$** across **model families and cloud regions** using a repeatable method.
- Emphasizes **reproducibility and variance controls** (not cherry-picked wins).
- Helps teams make better decisions about **where to run**, **which model to choose**, and **how to tune serving** to hit SLOs at a sane unit cost.

**Core promise:** predictable, observable, and economical inference across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

---
## Positioning statement (internal)
Redwood Inference is the developer-first inference platform optimized for **production economics**—helping teams consistently hit latency and reliability targets **at the lowest sustainable unit cost**, across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

---
## Messaging hierarchy (use this structure)
### 1) Hero message (landing page / first slide)
**“Latency per dollar: benchmarked across models and regions for real production economics.”**

Approved variants:
- “Production economics for LLM inference: latency, cost, and throughput—measured across regions.”
- “A reproducible benchmark for the metric teams actually operate against: performance per dollar.”

### 2) Subhead (what makes this credible)
“Built with explicit workloads, controlled settings, and variance analysis—so teams can interpret results responsibly and reproduce them.”

### 3) Proof points (pick 2–3)
- **Reproducible methodology:** clearly defined workloads, distributions, and measurement windows.
- **Region-by-region reporting:** results shown per region so teams can plan for residency and user geography.
- **Variance + constraints disclosed:** we highlight confidence/variance and avoid absolute claims.
- **Actionable knobs:** results map to decisions teams can actually make (routing, caching/batching policy, deployment mode).

### 4) Primary CTA (choose based on segment)
- PLG: “Try it on Hosted API (free credits) →”
- Sales-assisted: “Book a production economics consult →”
- Enterprise/regulated: “Ask about Dedicated/Private + residency controls →”

---
## Key narratives (the 3 pillars)
### Pillar A — Production economics is the new competitive advantage
**Narrative:** The fastest path to differentiation is not “which model,” it’s “how efficiently can you serve it.” Teams win on latency SLOs, reliability, and unit cost.

Talk track (SE/AEs):
- “In production, you don’t buy a model; you buy an *outcome*—p95 latency at a cost envelope.”
- “Latency/$ is a way to make the tradeoff explicit rather than hand-wavy.”

### Pillar B — Credibility through method, not marketing
**Narrative:** Benchmarks are only useful if they’re interpretable. We publish our method, variance handling, and constraints.

Talk track:
- “We don’t ask you to trust a single chart—we show you how the test was run and what might change the result.”

### Pillar C — One platform across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private
**Narrative:** Regardless of where you need to deploy, Redwood provides a consistent runtime + operational layer so performance is predictable and tunable.

Talk track:
- “Even if you start on Hosted, you can keep the same interface and move to Dedicated/Private when you need isolation, SLAs, or residency.”

---
## Headline stats (approved types + how to cite)
Because this report is public-facing, **headline stats must be framed as measurements under specified conditions** and must not imply universal superiority.

### Approved headline stat categories
Use only stats that appear in the latest approved report draft and/or the public table.

1) **Coverage / scope stats** (safe default)
- “We benchmarked multiple model families across North America, Europe, and APAC regions.”
- “We report p50/p95 latency, throughput, cost per 1M tokens, and Latency/$ per region.”

2) **Variance / rigor stats** (credibility builders)
- “Runs are repeated and variance is reported/used to gate re-runs.”
- “We separate warmup from measurement windows and disclose caching/batching policy.”

3) **Decision-driving deltas** (only if directly supported in the report)
- “Latency/$ varies meaningfully by region and workload; region selection can change the economics even when the model is the same.”
- “Different models can have similar cost but very different p95 latency profiles at the same concurrency.”

### How to cite headline stats (required pattern)
When presenting a stat, include:
- **Metric + workload** (chat vs embeddings)
- **Region(s)**
- **Latency percentile** (p50/p95)
- **Test conditions qualifier**

Approved citation template:
> “In our published Latency/$ benchmark (chat workload, [region], [concurrency profile]), we observed [result]. Results depend on workload and settings; see methodology for details.”

---
## What Latency/$ means (explainers)
### One-sentence definition (approved)
**Latency per dollar (Latency/$) measures how much latency you ‘buy’ with each dollar of inference spend—capturing the performance-cost tradeoff in a single, comparable metric.**

### Engineer-friendly explanation (use in technical discovery)
- “You can optimize for lowest latency by throwing more GPUs at the problem, or optimize for lowest cost by pushing utilization up. Latency/$ helps quantify the middle ground.”
- “It’s not replacing p95 latency or $/1M tokens; it’s a way to compare configurations when you need both constraints.”

Engineer Q&A snippets:
- **Q: Is Latency/$ just a marketing metric?**
  - “No. We still report p50/p95, throughput, and cost explicitly. Latency/$ is derived from those to make tradeoffs easier to see.”
- **Q: Does it account for quality?**
  - “No—quality is orthogonal. We recommend using Latency/$ alongside your evals/acceptance tests.”

### Procurement/finance-friendly explanation (use with buying committee)
- “We’re translating performance into unit economics: how much user-visible latency reduction you get per dollar.”
- “It helps compare options fairly when pricing models differ and when regions have different infrastructure costs.”

Procurement Q&A snippets:
- **Q: Does this predict our exact cost?**
  - “It predicts under defined test conditions. We use it to establish a baseline and then validate against your workload in a short pilot.”

---
## Approved language (copy/paste)
### Elevator pitch (15 seconds)
“Redwood Inference helps teams run LLMs with predictable latency and cost. We published a Latency per Dollar benchmark across models and regions so engineering teams can make real production economics decisions—based on reproducible measurements, not anecdotes.”

### Longer pitch (45–60 seconds)
“Teams are past the demo phase—what matters now is production economics: hitting p95 latency and reliability targets at a unit cost the business can support. Redwood Inference publishes a Latency/$ benchmark across models and regions with an explicit methodology and variance controls. The goal is to help teams choose regions, model families, and serving configurations more confidently—and to show how Redwood’s platform makes those tradeoffs observable and tunable across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.”

### Safe comparison framing (when asked “how do you stack up?”)
Approved:
- “The report is designed to be interpretable rather than provocative—same workloads, disclosed settings, and region-by-region results.”
- “If you want an apples-to-apples comparison for your workload, we can run a short joint evaluation using the same harness.”

Not approved:
- “We’re the fastest / cheapest across the board.”
- “Vendor X is misleading because…” (route to competitive FAQ + approvals)

---
## Do / Don’t list (claims and field behavior)
### DO
- Do say: “**In our benchmark conditions…**” and point to the methodology.
- Do show: p95 + throughput + cost together, not a single metric in isolation.
- Do emphasize: “**region-by-region** results” and “**workload-dependent** outcomes.”
- Do offer: a reproduction path (or a lightweight customer-specific pilot) when skepticism is high.
- Do use: “better *under these conditions*” instead of “best.”

### DON’T
- Don’t claim universal superiority (“best,” “always,” “guaranteed savings”).
- Don’t quote numbers from stale drafts or internal tables not in the final approved public materials.
- Don’t hide constraints (sequence lengths, concurrency, caching/batching policy). If asked, answer or share the appendix.
- Don’t imply Latency/$ is a quality metric.
- Don’t name competitors in writing unless it’s an approved competitive asset.

### Red-flag phrases to avoid (replace with approved alternatives)
- Avoid: “proves” → Use: “suggests,” “we observed,” “under these conditions.”
- Avoid: “real-world” (absolute) → Use: “production-representative workloads” with definition.
- Avoid: “apples-to-apples” unless conditions are truly identical → Use: “controlled settings; see methodology.”

## Persona-based talk tracks (quick pick)
| Persona | What they care about | What to say | What to offer |
|---|---|---|---|
| ML/Platform Engineer | p95 latency, throughput, failure modes, reproducibility | “We publish method + variance so you can interpret results. Latency/$ is derived from p95 + cost.” | Reproduction guide + pilot with their prompts and concurrency profile |
| Product Engineer | fast integration, predictable performance | “Same API across models/regions; report helps pick a sensible default for your region.” | Hosted API quickstart + suggested model shortlist |
| Head of Eng / CTO | roadmap risk, operating cost | “Serving is the differentiator now; this report gives a defensible baseline for planning.” | Cost/latency review + Dedicated/Private roadmap overview |
| Procurement / Finance | unit economics, contract predictability | “We’re making performance-cost tradeoffs explicit; we can validate with a pilot and then move to reserved capacity if needed.” | Dedicated capacity proposal + pricing model walkthrough |
| Security / Compliance | data handling, residency | “Results are reported by region; we support Dedicated/Private with residency and isolation controls.” | Security FAQ + architecture overview |

## Objections we expect (and the approved responses)
### Objection: “Benchmarks never match my workload.”
Response:
- “Agreed—benchmarks are baselines, not predictions. That’s why we publish the full methodology and encourage reproduction. Let’s run a small pilot with your prompts, sequence lengths, and concurrency.”

### Objection: “Latency/$ is a weird metric. Why not just cost?”
Response:
- “Cost alone can hide a bad user experience. Latency/$ is not a replacement—it’s a shortcut to compare tradeoffs when you need *both* latency and cost to be reasonable.”

### Objection: “Regions differ; isn’t this just infrastructure pricing?”
Response:
- “Region differences are real and are part of what teams must plan for. We publish results per region specifically so teams can choose residency and routing policies intentionally.”

---
## How to use this in the field (practical guidance)
### Discovery call (recommended sequence)
1) Establish their constraint: “What’s your p95 SLO, typical output tokens, and target cost per message?”
2) Use the report to set a baseline: “Here’s what we observe for similar conditions in your region.”
3) Offer next step: “We can validate with your workload and then tune batching/caching/routing to meet your SLO.”

### Email/LinkedIn outbound (approved framing)
- Focus on credibility + usefulness, not a dunk:
  - “We published a reproducible Latency/$ benchmark across models and regions—happy to share the methodology and help map it to your workload.”

### Procurement step (approved framing)
- “We’ll validate economics in a pilot, then lock predictability with Dedicated capacity if needed.”

## Appendix: Glossary (field-safe)
- **p50 / p95 latency:** median and tail response times; p95 is typically closer to user experience under load.
- **Throughput:** tokens/sec (or requests/sec for embeddings) under a defined concurrency profile.
- **Cost per 1M tokens:** normalized spend for generation under stated assumptions.
- **Latency/$:** derived metric that combines latency and cost to express “performance per unit spend.”

(For formulas and exact computation details, refer to the methodology page listed in Related Pages.)
